mcq.section: The Shape of Your Data Decides the Type
mcq.prompt: A lookup returns either an order or nothing. Which of these representations can express a contradictory state — a `false` status sitting beside an apparently valid Order?
choices: std::variant<Order, NotFound>
std::optional<Order>
std::pair<Order, bool>
std::expected<Order, NotFound>
mcq.explain: A pair is a product type: both members always exist, so nothing stops the Order half from looking valid while the bool says the lookup failed. The sum, nullable and result forms each store exactly one of the two possibilities, so the contradiction is unrepresentable. The pair form is tempting because it is the oldest idiom and needs no header, but it moves the invariant into a convention the caller has to obey.

mcq.section: The Shape of Your Data Decides the Type
mcq.prompt: A parser must report *why* it failed, and the calling path must not throw. Which vocabulary type states that contract?
choices: std::expected<T, E>
std::optional<T>
std::any
std::variant<T, T>
mcq.explain: std::expected<T, E> carries either the value or a caller-chosen error type, as an ordinary return value the caller tests. std::optional is the tempting near-miss: it also models failure, but it records only that the value is absent and destroys the reason. std::variant<T, T> is not even well-formed as a design — duplicated alternatives can only be reached by index, not by type.

mcq.prompt: Iterating a std::map with `for (auto [symbol, book] : books)` instead of `for (const auto& [symbol, book] : books)` does what?
choices: Nothing different; structured bindings always alias the source
Copies each map entry, so writes through the names do not reach the map
Fails to compile, because value_type contains a const Key
Iterates in an unspecified order rather than key order
mcq.explain: The binding declaration's `auto` versus `const auto&` decides whether a hidden copy of the whole element is made; the names are then introduced for that object's members. The copy compiles fine — copy-initialising a `std::pair<const std::string, OrderBook>` is legal — it just silently detaches the names from the container. Map iteration order is unrelated and is always key order.

mcq.prompt: What does `std::tie(left.price, left.sequence) < std::tie(right.price, right.sequence)` compute?
choices: true only when both price and sequence compare less
A copy of both members, then a memberwise comparison
Whether the two structs have the same address
A lexicographic comparison: price first, sequence only when prices are equal
mcq.explain: std::tie builds a tuple of lvalue references, and tuple's relational operators compare element by element in order, stopping at the first difference — exactly lexicographic ordering. Requiring *both* comparisons to be less would not even be a strict weak ordering. Note also that tie references rather than copies, which is why it is cheap enough for a hot comparison operator.

mcq.prompt: `opt` is a disengaged `std::optional<Order>`. What do `*opt` and `opt.value()` do?
choices: Both throw std::bad_optional_access
Both are undefined behaviour
`*opt` is undefined behaviour; `opt.value()` throws std::bad_optional_access
`*opt` throws; `opt.value()` returns a value-initialised Order
mcq.explain: operator* is the unchecked accessor: it is undefined behaviour on a disengaged optional, and typically reads whatever bytes the inline storage happens to hold. .value() is the checked accessor and throws std::bad_optional_access. Assuming operator* checks is the usual mistake — reach for it only after control flow has already proved engagement.

mcq.prompt: How do you express an optional *reference* to an Order that the caller does not own?
choices: Use a raw `Order*`; std::optional<T&> does not exist
std::optional<Order&>
std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<Order>> is the only legal spelling
std::expected<Order&, std::nullopt_t>
mcq.explain: The standard does not provide std::optional<T&>, so the chapter's rule is that a nullable non-owning reference is spelled `Order*` — a pointer already has a null state and borrowing semantics. std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<Order>> does compile, but it is a heavier spelling of the same pointer and forces every reader through `.value().get()`.

mcq.prompt: In a monadic chain, what distinguishes `and_then(f)` from `transform(f)`?
choices: and_then runs on absence; transform runs on the engaged value
and_then's callable returns another optional; transform's callable returns a plain value that gets wrapped
and_then is evaluated eagerly; transform is lazy
transform can change the contained type; and_then cannot
mcq.explain: and_then composes a function that can itself fail — it returns optional<U>, and the chain does not double-wrap. transform maps a value to a value and the library re-wraps the result. Both run only on the engaged path, so "and_then handles absence" is the confusion to avoid; or_else is the one that handles absence. Both can change the contained type.

mcq.section: `std::expected`: A Value or a Typed Failure
mcq.prompt: How does a function returning `std::expected<Price, PriceError>` produce the failure state?
choices: return PriceError::negative;
return std::nullopt;
throw PriceError::negative;
return std::unexpected(PriceError::negative);
mcq.explain: std::unexpected wraps the error so that the return statement unambiguously selects the error alternative. Returning the bare enumerator is the tempting spelling, but it is ambiguous in general — nothing distinguishes an error value from a value of type T when the two types are convertible — so the library requires the tag. std::nullopt belongs to optional, which has no error payload at all.

mcq.section: `std::expected`: A Value or a Typed Failure
mcq.prompt: What is `std::expected<void, SendError>` for?
choices: Storing an error without any way to signal success
A command that either succeeds with no payload or fails with a reason
A function that must be declared noexcept
An expected whose error type is deduced at the call site
mcq.explain: The specialisation keeps the success/error tag but carries no value on the success side, so `if (!sent) { ... sent.error() ... }` reads the same as for a value-returning call. It still signals success — testing the object as a bool is the whole point. Returning a bare bool instead is the tempting alternative and it throws away the failure reason.

mcq.section: `std::expected`: A Value or a Typed Failure
mcq.prompt: A low-level parser returns `std::expected<Price, PriceError>` and your subsystem's public API must return `std::expected<Price, FeedError>`. Which operation performs that adaptation?
choices: and_then, because it can return a differently typed expected
transform, because it maps the value
transform_error, because it maps the error and preserves the success type
or_else, because it is the only one that sees the error
mcq.explain: transform_error rewrites the error representation while leaving Price untouched — exactly the boundary translation the chapter's "one error vocabulary per boundary" rule asks for. or_else also sees the error, but its callable must return a full expected, so you would rebuild the success type by hand for no benefit. transform only maps the success value and never runs on the error path.

mcq.prompt: A `std::variant<Trade, Quote, Heartbeat>` currently holds a Quote and code calls `std::get<Trade>(message)`. What happens?
choices: It throws std::bad_variant_access
It is undefined behaviour
It returns a value-initialised Trade
It fails to compile, since the active alternative is not known statically
mcq.explain: std::get is the checked type-based accessor and throws std::bad_variant_access on a mismatch — a variant is a *type-safe* tagged union precisely because a wrong-alternative read is not silent. Reading an inactive union member would be undefined behaviour, but that is a raw union, not a variant. `std::get_if<Trade>(&message)` is the non-throwing form and returns nullptr instead.

mcq.prompt: A visitor passed to std::visit handles Trade and Quote but not Heartbeat, and has no generic fallback. What happens?
choices: std::visit throws std::bad_variant_access at runtime when a Heartbeat arrives
The Heartbeat case is silently skipped
The program fails to compile
The visitor is called with a default-constructed Trade
mcq.explain: std::visit requires the visitor to be invocable for every alternative and to return a common type, so a missing case is a compile error — exhaustiveness becomes a checked property rather than a runtime hazard. That is the main reason to prefer visit over a chain of holds_alternative tests, which silently falls through when a new alternative is added to the variant.

mcq.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts `variant` plus visit with a virtual base-class hierarchy?
choices: variant dispatch is always faster because it avoids a vtable
variant stores alternatives out of line, so its wrapper is pointer-sized
variant supports adding new message kinds from independent libraries without recompiling
variant's alternative set is closed at compile time, and each object is as large as the largest alternative
mcq.explain: Those two properties are the real trade: the closed list is what makes exhaustive visitation checkable, and inline storage is what makes every Message as big as its largest member even when it holds a tiny Heartbeat. The performance claim is the tempting one and the chapter explicitly refuses it — representation, branch prediction and surrounding allocation decide, not the dispatch mechanism. Open extension is precisely what the virtual hierarchy offers and variant does not.

mcq.prompt: A `std::any` was constructed from an `int` holding 3. What does `std::any_cast<long>(value)` do?
choices: Returns 3L, applying the usual integer conversion
Throws std::bad_any_cast, because the stored type is exactly int
Returns 0, since the types do not match
Fails to compile
mcq.explain: any_cast matches the stored type exactly through runtime type identification; no implicit conversion is attempted, so long is simply a different type from int and the reference form throws. The pointer form `std::any_cast<long>(&value)` is the non-throwing alternative and returns nullptr. Expecting a numeric conversion is the classic any bug because the same code with `int` works perfectly.

mcq.prompt: A `std::vector<std::reference_wrapper<Order>>` is built from a `std::deque<Order>`, and the deque is then destroyed while the vector is still in use. What is the situation?
choices: Every wrapper dangles exactly as a raw reference would
The wrappers are safe: reference_wrapper keeps the referent alive
The vector detects the destruction and becomes empty
The wrappers are safe as long as the vector is never resized
mcq.explain: reference_wrapper is a copyable, assignable *view*; it stores the address and owns nothing, so its lifetime rules are the reference's lifetime rules. The reason it exists is that raw references cannot be stored in containers or reassigned, not that it adds ownership. Resizing the vector is irrelevant — the danger is the referents' lifetime, not the wrappers' storage.

mcq.prompt: A 64-bit mask uses bit *i* to mean "price level *i* has orders". Which `<bit>` function gives the number of occupied levels?
choices: std::countr_zero
std::bit_floor
std::popcount
std::has_single_bit
mcq.explain: std::popcount counts the set bits, which is the number of occupied levels. std::countr_zero is the tempting neighbour and answers a different question — how many zero bits sit below the lowest set bit, which is the index of the *best* occupied level. Both map to a single machine instruction on mainstream targets.

mcq.prompt: What does `std::countr_zero(std::uint64_t{0})` return, and what should the caller do about it?
choices: It is undefined behaviour for a zero input
0, so an empty mask reports level 0
-1, which is a convenient sentinel
64, which is not a valid level index, so check for an empty mask first
mcq.explain: For an all-zero value the function returns the bit width, 64 — well-defined, but out of range as an index, so indexing a 64-entry level array with it walks off the end. Assuming it returns 0 is the dangerous misreading, because 0 is a *valid* index and the bug becomes a silent wrong answer rather than a crash. Test the mask against zero before using the result.

mcq.prompt: When can `std::bitset<64>::to_ulong()` fail?
choices: Never; the compile-time size guarantees the conversion fits
When a set bit does not fit in unsigned long — it throws std::overflow_error
When the bitset is all zeros
Only in a constant expression
mcq.explain: The bitset's compile-time width says nothing about the width of unsigned long on the target — on LLP64 Windows it is 32 bits — so bit 40 being set makes the conversion impossible and to_ulong throws std::overflow_error. Assuming the sizes always match is a portability bug that never fires on the developer's LP64 machine. Use to_ullong, or keep the mask in a fixed-width integer.

mcq.prompt: A lane-wise SIMD sum of the same float array gives a slightly different total than a left-to-right scalar loop. Why?
choices: Floating-point addition is not associative, and lanes change the grouping of the partial sums
SIMD registers use a narrower significand than scalar registers
The masked tail elements are dropped
std::simd::reduce rounds its result to the nearest representable float
mcq.explain: Each lane accumulates its own partial sum and reduce combines them at the end, so intermediate roundings happen in a different order than a sequential accumulation — and IEEE addition is not associative, so the totals can differ in the last bits. The lanes have the same precision as scalar floats; nothing is truncated. A backtest that must reproduce bit-for-bit has to pin its reduction order, flags, and target.

mcq.prompt: What is wrong with `venue = std::rand() % venue_count;`?
choices: It fails to compile without seeding first
std::rand is not thread-safe, which is the only defect
Unless venue_count divides the engine's range evenly, some venues become more likely — plus rand's global state and weak quality
It always returns the same venue because rand is deterministic
mcq.explain: Modulo bias is the concrete correctness bug: the leftover partial cycle at the top of the range makes low remainders slightly more likely. std::uniform_int_distribution<int>{0, venue_count - 1} handles the range without bias. Determinism is not the problem — a fixed seed is the *desired* default for backtests; the problem is rand's global mutable state, possibly small range, and inadequate quality.

mcq.prompt: Two runs of a Monte Carlo simulation use `std::mt19937_64 engine{42}` and `std::normal_distribution<double>{0.0, 1.0}`, one built with libstdc++ and one with libc++. What is guaranteed?
choices: Identical draws, because the engine and seed are specified by the standard
The engine's bit sequence matches, but the distribution's output may differ because its algorithm is unspecified
Nothing at all; mt19937_64 is implementation-defined
Identical draws only if std::random_device is also used
mcq.explain: The standard specifies mt19937_64's recurrence exactly, so its raw bit stream is reproducible across libraries. It does not specify how normal_distribution turns those bits into normal variates — Box-Muller and ziggurat consume different numbers of bits — so the resulting doubles can differ. Cross-library reproducibility of *distributions* requires shipping your own distribution code.

mcq.prompt: Which clock should time the interval between packet arrival and order transmission?
choices: std::chrono::steady_clock, because it never moves backward
std::chrono::system_clock, because its epoch is Unix time
std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, because its name promises the finest tick
Either steady_clock or system_clock; they differ only in epoch
mcq.explain: steady_clock is monotonic, so an NTP correction or an administrator setting the date cannot make the measured interval negative or distorted. system_clock is the tempting answer because its epoch is meaningful, but a meaningful epoch is exactly what you *don't* need for an elapsed time — and it can jump. high_resolution_clock is only an implementation-defined alias for one of the other two, so its name guarantees nothing.

mcq.prompt: `std::chrono::milliseconds whole = 1500us;` does what?
choices: Compiles and stores 1, truncating toward zero
Compiles and stores 2, rounding to nearest
Fails to compile, because the conversion can lose precision and must be an explicit duration_cast
Compiles and stores 1500, since the count is copied unchanged
mcq.explain: Duration conversions are implicit only when the target's unit ratio can represent every source value exactly — milliseconds cannot represent 1500 microseconds — so the library refuses the conversion. `duration_cast<milliseconds>(1500us)` makes the truncation explicit and yields 1. Expecting a silent truncation is the C-style habit chrono exists to break: the compiler asks you to admit the loss.

mcq.prompt: Why does the chapter tell you never to use std::chrono::high_resolution_clock?
choices: It is deprecated in C++23
It requires linking an extra library on most platforms
Its now() is measurably slower than steady_clock::now()
It is an implementation-defined alias, so it guarantees neither monotonicity nor a better timer
mcq.explain: The standard permits high_resolution_clock to be an alias for steady_clock or system_clock, so the same source can be monotonic on one platform and jump on another — a portability trap dressed up as a performance promise. It is not deprecated and needs no extra library; the objection is semantic, not mechanical. Choose the property you need by naming steady_clock or system_clock explicitly.

mcq.prompt: You need the UTC instant of the 09:30 New York open for an arbitrary session date. What is wrong with adding a fixed five-hour offset?
choices: Nothing, provided the date is a weekday
The offset changes across daylight-saving transitions, so a fixed constant is wrong for part of the year
sys_time cannot represent an offset from local time
Five hours is the wrong constant; four hours is correct
mcq.explain: America/New_York is UTC-5 in winter and UTC-4 in summer, and the transition dates themselves move, so any hardcoded constant silently produces an hour-wrong timestamp for months at a time. std::chrono::zoned_time applies the tz database rules for the specific local time and converts to sys_time correctly. Picking the "other" constant just moves the wrong half of the year.

reading.explain: A structured binding names the parts of whatever object the declaration introduced, and `auto [part, count]` introduces a *copy* of the map entry — so the first loop doubles two temporaries that are destroyed at the end of each iteration and the map never sees it. `auto&` binds to the entry itself, so the second loop really does increment, leaving 4+1 and 9+1. The tempting reading is that the names are references because they look like ones; the ampersand is on the declaration, not on the names, and forgetting it produces a loop that compiles, runs, and does nothing. Note the keys are unchanged either way: a map's key half is const.

The Boolean conversion on an optional reports engagement, never the value inside, so an engaged optional holding 0 tests true — which is the entire reason optional exists rather than a sentinel. The trap is in the third column: value_or(0) maps 'absent' onto the same 0 that 'settled at zero' already produces, so the comparison is 1 and the distinction the type was protecting has been thrown away at the point of use. The tempting reading is that `if (settled_zero)` would be false because the payload is falsy — that is the behaviour of a bare int, and swapping in optional is what removes it. When zero is a legitimate value, branch on has_value() and keep the two cases apart.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: get_if is exception-free precisely because it reports a mismatch through its return value: asked for the int alternative of a variant currently holding a std::string, it returns nullptr, and dereferencing that is undefined behaviour the sanitizer reports as a null pointer dereference. The first access is fine; the second is the bug. The tempting reading is that 'does not throw' means 'safe', so get_if can replace std::get without further thought — the two differ in *how* they report the mismatch, and get_if moves the obligation onto the caller. Test the pointer, or use std::visit and let the compiler prove every alternative is handled.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: std::visit must have one return type for the whole call: the visitor is instantiated once per alternative, and here those instantiations return int, double and std::string, which have no single common type the call could adopt. The compiler rejects it rather than picking one. The tempting reading is that a generic lambda makes a visitor automatically correct — it does make it exhaustive, which is a different property, and exhaustiveness is worth nothing if the alternatives cannot agree on a result. Give the lambda an explicit return type that every alternative converts to, such as `-> std::string` with a conversion in the body, or have the visitor produce its output as a side effect and return void.

reading.section: `std::expected`: A Value or a Typed Failure
reading.explain: transform maps the success side and leaves the failure side alone: the good field becomes 42, while the bad one never calls the lambda and keeps carrying Fault::not_a_number all the way out, which is what distinguishes expected from optional — the reason survives the pipeline. value_or supplies -1 for the failed one, and error() is still readable afterwards because transform did not consume or translate it. The tempting reading is that transform must be given something to do for the error case, or that value_or discards the error: the error is only replaced by transform_error, and only read by error() on an object that has none.

any_cast matches the stored type exactly, with no conversions and no relatives: an int is not retrievable as a long even though every int fits in one, so the first two columns are 0 and 1. The assignment then stores whatever the expression's type is, and a string literal is a const char*, not a std::string — so asking for std::string fails and asking for const char* succeeds. The tempting reading is that assigning the literal stores a string because that is what it looks like; type erasure erases the static type but records it precisely, and the conversion that would normally happen at a std::string parameter never gets a chance to. The pointer form used here reports the mismatch as nullptr; the value form would throw std::bad_any_cast.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The first line prints fine — count() and test() work at any width. to_ulong() is the one that cannot: it throws std::overflow_error whenever a set bit lies outside the range of unsigned long, and bit 100 does, so the exception escapes main and the program terminates. The tempting reading is that the conversion silently truncates to the low bits, the way a narrowing integer conversion would; bitset chose to report the loss instead. The size of the bitset is a compile-time constant, but whether the *value* fits is a runtime property, which is why this cannot be a compile error. Extract a specific word (to_ullong on a narrower slice, or a shifted-and-masked sub-bitset) when a C API needs one.

Subtracting two durations converts both to their common type, and the common type of milliseconds and microseconds is the finer one, so `left` is 600 microseconds and its count() is 600 rather than 0.6 — a duration's count is meaningless without its unit, which is exactly why the unit is in the type. duration_cast then truncates toward zero and reports 0 whole milliseconds, while round gives the nearest, 1. The tempting reading is that budget - spent is 'obviously in milliseconds' because that is how the budget was written, and that the remaining time is therefore 0 or 1 depending on which cast you happen to use. Compare durations directly, as the last column does, instead of comparing counts.

writing.prompt: A log index is keyed by `LogKey{int severity; std::string source; long line;}`. Write `operator<` ordering by severity, then source, then line, and `emit(const std::tuple<int, std::string, long>&)` that calls an existing `write_row(int, std::string, long)` with the stored arguments. Contract: no chain of if-statements in the comparator, and `emit` must not name any element position.
checklist: The comparator is a single expression built from std::tie on both sides
The two tie calls list the members in the same order, so the comparison is lexicographic
No <= or >= appears anywhere in the comparator
emit uses std::apply and never std::get<0>, <1> or <2>
A comment states why the named struct is preferable to the tuple at an interface
writing.notes: std::tie makes a tuple of references, so nothing is copied even though `source` is a std::string -- writing std::make_tuple here would copy both strings on every comparison, inside a sort that runs the comparator O(N log N) times. If the type owns all its members and the default member order is the order you want, `auto operator<=>(const LogKey&) const = default;` says the same thing in one line.

writing.prompt: A config map is `std::map<std::string, std::string>`. Write `lookup(cfg, key)` returning `std::optional<std::string>`, `as_seconds(const std::string&)` returning `std::optional<int>` for a strictly positive decimal number, and `timeout_seconds(cfg)` which is their composition, clamped to at most 300 and defaulting to 30 when anything is missing or malformed. Contract: `timeout_seconds` must contain no `if`, no `has_value()`, and no dereference.
checklist: lookup returns std::nullopt for a missing key rather than an empty string
as_seconds rejects a non-numeric or non-positive value with std::nullopt
timeout_seconds is a single monadic chain: and_then, transform, value_or
and_then is used for the stage that itself returns an optional, transform for the stage that does not
The 300 clamp is inside transform, so it applies only to a value that was actually present
writing.notes: Using transform where and_then belongs is the usual slip: it would produce an optional<optional<int>>, which then tests engaged whenever the *outer* lookup succeeded, defeating the check. Note also that value_or evaluates its argument unconditionally -- fine for the literal 30, wasteful or wrong if the default were an expensive call or one with side effects.

writing.prompt: A spreadsheet cell is `std::variant<std::monostate, double, std::string>` — blank, numeric, or text. Write `describe(const Cell&)` returning a `std::string` that names which alternative is active, and `column_total(const std::vector<Cell>&)` summing only the numeric cells. Contract: neither function may call `std::get`, `index()`, or `holds_alternative`, and adding a fourth alternative later must make the code fail to compile rather than silently ignore it.
checklist: Both functions dispatch with std::visit
The visitor has one call operator per alternative; no generic `auto` catch-all
std::get, index() and holds_alternative appear nowhere
describe returns one type from every alternative, so the visit has a common return type
std::monostate is handled explicitly as the blank cell
writing.notes: Each lambda in `describe` returns std::string rather than a string literal, because a visitor whose alternatives return const char* and std::string has no common return type and will not compile -- the same failure the reading exercise on this section shows. Putting monostate first in the alternative list is also what makes a default-constructed Cell blank rather than 0.0.

writing.prompt: Given `std::vector<std::string>& lines` holding a log file, write `longest_first(lines, n)` returning the `n` longest lines ordered longest-first. Contract: no `std::string` may be copied, the caller's vector must be left in its original order, and the result must let the caller edit the lines in place.
checklist: Returns std::vector<std::reference_wrapper<std::string>>, not a vector of strings or of indices
The wrappers are what get sorted; lines itself is never reordered
The projection or comparator reaches the string through .get()
Truncates to n only after selecting, and handles n larger than lines.size()
A comment states that every wrapper dangles if `lines` is destroyed or reallocated
writing.notes: A reference_wrapper is assignable and copyable, which is the whole reason it can live in a container where a plain std::string& cannot. Because the elements are references, a caller assigning through refs[0].get() edits the original line -- convenient, and the reason to hand back const references (std::cref) unless mutation is part of the contract.

writing.prompt: A worker pool tracks 64 slots in a `std::uint64_t busy` mask, bit `i` set meaning slot `i` is in use. Write `claim(std::uint64_t& busy)` returning the lowest free slot index or -1 when the pool is full, `release(std::uint64_t& busy, int slot)`, and `load_percent(std::uint64_t busy)`. Contract: no loops, no division by a non-constant, and every shift must be provably in range.
checklist: claim inspects the complement of the mask, not the mask itself
The full-pool case is tested before countr_zero is used as an index
Shifts are written on a std::uint64_t operand (e.g. std::uint64_t{1} << slot), not on int 1
release validates the slot index before shifting
load_percent uses std::popcount rather than a counting loop
writing.notes: Writing `1 << slot` would compute in int and be undefined for slot >= 31; the std::uint64_t{1} spelling is not pedantry, it is the difference between a mask and a bug that only fires on the high slots. For a flag set that does not fit a machine word, std::bitset<N> gives the same operations by name -- at the cost of to_ulong() being able to throw.

writing.prompt: Write a `Shuffler` class that puts a playlist into a random order. Contract: two Shufflers built with the same seed must produce identical orderings, the same object must produce a *different* ordering on its second call, the seed must be readable back for a bug report, and no engine may be constructed per call.
checklist: The engine is a member, constructed once and seeded from the constructor argument
The seed is stored and exposed through an accessor
shuffle uses std::ranges::shuffle (or std::shuffle) with the member engine, never std::rand
The engine is passed by reference so its state advances between calls
A comment notes that a fixed seed is what makes a failing run replayable
writing.notes: std::random_device belongs at the boundary where nondeterminism is genuinely wanted -- seed from it once and *print the value you got*, so the run is still reproducible afterwards. Note also that only the engine sequence is standardised: distributions may be implemented differently across libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC, so a seed reproduces a run on one toolchain, not across three.

writing.prompt: Write a `Budget` class for a request handler: constructed with an allowance, it answers `remaining()` and `expired()`. Contract: it must measure elapsed time correctly across a wall-clock adjustment, `remaining()` must return a duration rather than a number, a caller passing a `std::chrono::seconds` allowance must compile while one passing a bare `int` must not, and each check must read the clock once.
checklist: steady_clock is used, and system_clock and high_resolution_clock are not
The allowance parameter is a chrono duration type, so a bare int is rejected by the compiler
The deadline (or the start time point) is stored as a time_point, not as an integer count
remaining() returns a duration type, not a count
now() is called once per query, not twice
writing.notes: Storing the deadline rather than the start makes every query one subtraction and keeps the allowance out of the object entirely. Returning a duration matters as much as measuring one: a caller who receives an int has to guess the unit, and `remaining().count()` at the call site is where that guess would be made explicit -- or where duration_cast would truncate it deliberately.

writing.prompt: Options expire on the third Friday of the month. Write `nth_weekday(std::chrono::year_month, std::chrono::weekday, unsigned n)` returning `std::expected<std::chrono::year_month_day, CalendarError>` — the error case being a month with no fifth Friday. Contract: no month-length table, no leap-year arithmetic, and no manual day counting.
checklist: Builds the date from the calendar operators (year_month / weekday[n]), not by adding days
Validates with .ok() before converting, and returns the error otherwise
Converts through sys_days to produce a year_month_day
No hard-coded array of month lengths and no % 4 leap-year test
The error is a typed enumeration returned via std::unexpected, not a sentinel date
writing.notes: The same operators express the other common trading-calendar shapes: `2026y/July/last` for the month end, and `weekday{sys_days{date}}` to ask which day a date fell on. A session *time* is a separate problem -- an exchange open is a local time in a named zone, so it needs zoned_time and the tz database, and adding a fixed offset instead breaks on the daylight-saving boundary.
